passage:
At five, Madhav flopped on the floor ten minutes into a rainy afternoon. "I'm bored. What now?" Papa Vijay pulled out a big cloth, some clothes pegs and a torch. Madhav grumbled, then built a cave, and the afternoon was gone.
At fifteen, Madhav had begun building a small robot arm for the school fair in March. It was October. The first weeks were exciting. By December, he found the wiring dull and the arm still barely moved. One evening he pushed the tools aside. "This is so boring. I'll never finish." His friend Wasim looked at the pile. "You've done more than you think. Remember how it looked in October?" Madhav remembered the cave and how he had turned a flat afternoon into something he liked. He split the work into a small weekly goal, played music while he soldered, and stuck a photo of the first version above his desk. His science teacher stopped by. "Show me on Friday whatever you have." Madhav picked up the screwdriver and began again.

qa.q: In which month was the school fair for which Madhav was building the robot arm?
How does Madhav's way of meeting boredom at fifteen connect to what he did at five?
qa.a: At five he turned a flat afternoon into a cave with a cloth, pegs and a torch. At fifteen, during a months-long project, he met boredom with the same inventiveness, using small weekly goals and music, and kept going despite setbacks.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he pushed the tools aside and said it was so boring?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and doubtful about finishing, with the boredom of the wiring making the goal seem far away.

qa.q: What could Madhav do if progress on the robot arm slows down again?
qa.a: He can review his old photo and weekly goals, ask Wasim or the science teacher for a check-in, and take a short break before starting again.

grounding: A child's boredom turned into imagination (4068) and a teen sustaining effort on a months-long project despite boredom and setbacks (250).
